title: Trees
definition: A tree is a non-linear data structure that represents the hierarchical relationship between individual data items. It is a collection of nodes where each node has a value and a list of references to other nodes (children). The first node in the tree is called the root, and nodes without children are called leaves.
conceptExplanation: Trees represent hierarchical relationships. A tree consists of a root node, and each node can have zero or more child nodes. The maximum number of children a node can have is called the degree of the node. Nodes on the same level are called siblings. The length of the path from the root to a node is called the depth of that node. The height of the tree is the maximum depth of any node.
keyPoints: - Non-linear data structure - Hierarchical relationship - Root, parent, child, leaf - Recursive structure - Height and depth
importantTerminology: Tree, Root, Node, Edge, Leaf, Sibling, Depth, Height, Degree, Level
workingPrinciple: A tree starts at the root node. Each node contains data and references (pointers) to its child nodes. The last node(s) with no children are leaves. Operations include: traversal (visiting all nodes), search (finding a node), insertion (adding a node), and deletion (removing a node). Traversal methods include inorder, preorder, and postorder for binary trees.
realLifeExample: File directory structure, organization chart, HTML DOM tree, decision trees in machine learning
dsaExample: Binary search tree insertion, tree traversal (inorder, preorder, postorder), counting nodes, finding height
diagram: Binary tree: Root node with value, left child, and right child. Tree structure showing root, internal nodes, and leaf nodes at different levels.
algorithm:
Tree Traversal - Inorder:
1. Traverse left subtree
2. Visit root
3. Traverse right subtree

Tree Traversal - Preorder:
1. Visit root
2. Traverse left subtree
3. Traverse right subtree

Tree Traversal - Postorder:
1. Traverse left subtree
2. Traverse right subtree
3. Visit root
pseudocode:
BEGIN
  // Inorder Traversal\n  FUNCTION inorder(node)
    IF node != NULL
      inorder(node.left)
      PROCESS node.data
      inorder(node.right)
    END IF
  END FUNCTION

  // Preorder Traversal\n  FUNCTION preorder(node)
    IF node != NULL
      PROCESS node.data
      preorder(node.left)
      preorder(node.right)
    END IF
  END FUNCTION

  // Postorder Traversal\n  FUNCTION postorder(node)
    IF node != NULL
      postorder(node.left)
      postorder(node.right)
      PROCESS node.data
    END IF
  END FUNCTION
END
complexity:
Time: Depends on tree balance\n- Balanced BST: Search O(log n), Insert O(log n), Delete O(log n)\n- Unbalanced BST (worst case like linked list): O(n)
- Traversal: O(n) for all (inorder, preorder, postorder)
- Space: O(h) where h is tree height (recursion stack)

Height of balanced tree: O(log n)
Height of unbalanced tree: O(n)
applications: Binary search trees for efficient search, file systems, organizational charts, decision trees, expression trees
advantages: Hierarchical data representation, efficient search in BST, dynamic size, flexible structure
limitations: Performance depends on tree balance, unbalanced trees degrade to O(n), no built-in balancing in basic BST
commonMistakes: Not handling null pointers, incorrect recursive base case, infinite recursion in cyclic trees, forgetting to update root when inserting first node

fiveMarkQuestions.question: Explain tree data structure with terminologies and traversal algorithms.
fiveMarkQuestions.answer:
A tree is a non-linear data structure that represents hierarchical relationships. Key terminologies:

- Root: The topmost node in the tree
- Node: Contains data and references to children
- Parent: A node that has child nodes
- Child: A node referenced by a parent
- Sibling: Nodes with the same parent
- Leaf: A node with no children
- Edge: Connection between parent and child
- Depth: Length of path from root to node
- Height: Maximum depth among all nodes
- Level: Depth of a node + 1 (root is at level 1)

Binary Tree: A tree where each node has at most 2 children (left and right).

Traversal Methods:
1. Inorder: Left → Root → Right. For BST, gives nodes in sorted order.
2. Preorder: Root → Left → Right. Used for copying trees.
3. Postorder: Left → Right → Root. Used for deleting trees.

BST (Binary Search Tree): Left child < parent < right child. Operations: search, insert, delete - O(log n) on average for balanced BST.

tenMarkQuestions.question: Explain tree data structure with algorithms and applications.
tenMarkQuestions.answer:
Tree: 

A tree is a non-linear data structure representing hierarchical relationships. It consists of nodes connected by edges. The topmost node is the root. Each node has a value and references to child nodes. Nodes without children are leaves.

Key Terminologies:
- Degree: Maximum number of children a node can have
- Depth: Path length from root to node
- Height: Maximum depth in the tree
- Level: Root at level 1, children at level 2, etc.
- Sibling: Nodes with same parent

Binary Tree: Each node has at most 2 children. Common variations:
- Full binary tree: Every node has 0 or 2 children
- Complete binary tree: All levels full except last, filled left-to-right
- Balanced binary tree: Height difference between subtrees ≤ 1

Traversal Algorithms:
1. Inorder (Left-Root-Right): For BST gives sorted output. Recursive: process left subtree, then root, then right subtree.
2. Preorder (Root-Left-Right): Copy tree structure. Visit root first.
3. Postorder (Left-Right-Root): Delete tree. Visit root last.

Binary Search Tree (BST): Satisfies BST property - left child < parent < right child.
Operations:
- Search: Start at root, compare target with node value, go left if smaller, right if larger.
- Insert: Similar to search, add new node at appropriate position.
- Delete: Three cases: leaf node, node with one child, node with two children (replace with inorder successor/predecessor).

Complexity:
- Balanced BST: Search/Insert/Delete O(log n)
- Unbalanced BST: O(n) worst case (degenerate to linked list)
- Traversal: O(n) always
- Height: O(log n) balanced, O(n) unbalanced

Applications:
1. Binary Search Trees: Database indexing, symbol tables
2. Heap: Priority queue implementation
3. Expression Trees: Compilers, expression evaluation
4. Tries: String searching, autocomplete
5. Decision Trees: Machine learning, classification
6. File Systems: Directory structure
7. HTML DOM: Web page structure

Comparison: Trees vs Arrays/Linked Lists: Trees provide hierarchical structure and efficient search (BST) but use more memory for pointers.
